The number of steps it takes to get to a given piece of content should be kept as low as possible, but while still taking into account that users have different mental models, different navigation strategies and different tasks."},{"id":"M1:T42","text":"On splash screens, we'd rather avoid them, unless they actually give the user useful content or feedback on the state of the application. And if we do use one, there has to be a navigation option to skip it. Also, don't open unnecessary windows. Extra windows, new browser windows, pop-ups, should only open if that really supports what the user is doing. New windows can distract, confuse or get in the way of users for all sorts of reasons. They can sit on top of the main window and hide relevant information, they can make the navigation structure harder to understand mentally, which hurts both usability and accessibility, and the user has to take extra actions just to close the ones they didn't want."},{"id":"M1:T43","text":"Another one is robustness. The user interfaces should be as robust as possible as technology changes. That means older user agents should still be able to present content that uses newer technologies, and the content should be designed so it's usable with future technologies too."},{"id":"M1:T44","text":"Okay, got it."},{"id":"M1:T45","text":"From my side, opening and download times. Application pages need to be designed and built so opening and download times are acceptable across the expected range of technical contexts of use, for example the bandwidth between the application and the user. That matters most for frequently accessed pages, or pages that are key for navigation and exploration, like the home page. Then error messages need to be clear. Whether it's on the page itself or a dedicated error page, the message should say clearly why the error happened and, where possible, what the user can do to fix it. And users expect error messages in the same language as the user interface."},{"id":"M1:T46","text":"Right."},{"id":"M1:T47","text":"Text quality as well. Spelling and grammar in the text content should be good enough that they don't get in the way of readability. And within-page links should be clearly distinguishable from links that go to a different page. Typical actions would be manipulating application data, running searches, communication actions like opening a new e-mail window or starting a chat, and presentation actions like sorting a list of search results. And we want printable versions. If a document is too long, spread over several pages, or has a layout that doesn't suit online reading, there should be a printer-friendly version that prints it in a form the user finds acceptable, for example the expected layout, paper format or orientation."},{"id":"M1:T52","text":"Then page length. It should be chosen to support the main purpose and use of the page. Short pages generally work better for homepages, navigation pages or overview pages that people need to read quickly.
